1031 EXCHANGE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105

EXCHANGE DECLARATION
This exchange declaration describes a like-kind exchange under 26 U.S.C. § 1031 involving the following properties. Taxpayer: Jordan Alex Lee. Relinquished property: 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, legally described as Lot 5, Block 12, per map recorded in Book 40, Page 15, San Francisco County Records. Replacement property: 200 Elm St, Reno, NV 89501, legally described as Lot 8, Block 3, per map recorded in Book 22, Page 9, Washoe County Records. The relinquished property was transferred on October 1, 2026. The replacement property was identified on November 15, 2026. The exchange was completed, with receipt of the replacement property, on March 30, 2027. This declaration is a factual record of the properties and dates involved in this exchange. It does not itself determine whether this exchange qualifies for nonrecognition treatment under § 1031, whether the relinquished and replacement properties are of like kind, whether the identification and completion deadlines described elsewhere in this document were met, or whether any state reporting requirement applies to this exchange.

CORE NONRECOGNITION RULE FOR REAL PROPERTY EXCHANGES
Federal tax law states that no gain or loss is recognized for federal income tax purposes on the exchange of real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment, if that real property is exchanged solely for real property of like kind that is likewise to be held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment. This rule is codified at 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(1) and applies only to real property. Before 2018, an equivalent nonrecognition rule also reached exchanges of certain personal property. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 amended § 1031 to limit nonrecognition treatment to real property, substituting "real property" for "property" throughout subsection (a)(1); that amendment applies to exchanges completed after December 31, 2017, subject to a transition rule preserving prior law for an exchange where the property given up was disposed of on or before that date, or the exchange was underway pursuant to a written agreement entered into on or before that date.

  "No gain or loss shall be recognized on the exchange of real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment if such real property is exchanged solely for real property of like kind which is to be held either for productive use in a trade or business or for investment."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, core like-kind exchange nonrecognition rule for real property (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)
  "the amendments made by this section [amending this section] shall apply to exchanges completed after December 31, 2017"
  — Pub. L. 115-97, § 13303(c) (reproduced in Editorial Notes to 26 U.S.C. § 1031, Cornell LII text), Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, effective date of the real-property-only limitation (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)

Both citations below are drawn from the same law.cornell.edu page for 26 U.S.C. § 1031: the first quotes the codified text of subsection (a)(1) itself, and the second quotes the reproduced text of the uncodified effective-date provision of Pub. L. 115-97, § 13303(c) (the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), which appears on that same page as an editorial note rather than as codified Code text. They are treated here as one source, not independent corroboration, since both come from the single fetched page for this section. No case law was researched for this clause; the topic is resolved directly by unambiguous statutory text, and this research is primarily statutory/regulatory in nature.

THE "LIKE KIND" STANDARD FOR REAL PROPERTY
Treasury regulations interpreting § 1031 state that the words "like kind," as used in the statute, refer to the nature or character of property, not to its grade or quality. Applying that standard, the regulations state that whether real estate is improved or unimproved is not material, because that fact relates only to grade or quality, not to kind or class — so real property is broadly treated as like kind to other real property regardless of grade or quality. The regulations illustrate this with examples of qualifying like-kind exchanges: a taxpayer who is not a real estate dealer exchanging city real estate for a ranch or farm, and an exchange of improved real estate for unimproved real estate. This broad like-kind standard for real property comes from Treasury regulations, not from the text of § 1031 itself — the statute does not define "like kind" or state this grade-or-quality distinction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the words like kind have reference to the nature or character of the property and not to its grade or quality"
  — 26 C.F.R. § 1.1031(a)-1(b) (Cornell LII text), Treasury regulation, definition of "like kind" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.1031(a)-1)
  "a taxpayer who is not a dealer in real estate exchanges city real estate for a ranch or farm, or exchanges a leasehold of a fee with 30 years or more to run for real estate, or exchanges improved real estate for unimproved real estate"
  — 26 C.F.R. § 1.1031(a)-1(c) (Cornell LII text), Treasury regulation, examples of like-kind real property exchanges (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.1031(a)-1)
  Known gap: This is a federal Treasury regulation, used as evidence of how "like kind" is defined for real property under § 1031 — not tax advice about whether any specific two parcels of real property are like kind to one another in a given exchange. Both citations below are subsections — (b) and (c) — of the same regulation section, 26 C.F.R. § 1.1031(a)-1, and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This regulation's general definition and examples predate the 2017 real-property-only limitation and were written when § 1031 covered personal as well as real property, but a separate paragraph of the same regulation section, § 1.1031(a)-1(a)(3), cross-references this definition as continuing to apply to exchanges of real property after 2017. No case law was researched for this clause, consistent with this research being primarily statutory/regulatory rather than case-law-driven.

IDENTIFICATION AND EXCHANGE-COMPLETION DEADLINES
Federal tax law fixes deadlines, measured from the transfer of the relinquished property, for identifying and receiving replacement property in a § 1031 exchange. Under 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(3), property received by the taxpayer is treated as property that is not like-kind property — and so falls outside nonrecognition treatment — unless it is identified as replacement property on or before the day that is 45 days after the date the taxpayer transfers the relinquished property, and it is received by the earlier of the day that is 180 days after that transfer date, or the due date (taking extensions into account) of the taxpayer's tax return for the year in which the transfer of the relinquished property occurs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "such property is not identified as property to be received in the exchange on or before the day which is 45 days after the date on which the taxpayer transfers the property relinquished in the exchange"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, 45-day identification deadline (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)
  "the day which is 180 days after the date on which the taxpayer transfers the property relinquished in the exchange"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, 180-day exchange-completion deadline (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as evidence of the identification and completion deadlines § 1031 imposes generally — not tax advice about whether any specific taxpayer's exchange met these deadlines. Both citations below are subparagraphs — (A) and (B) — of the same statutory paragraph, § 1031(a)(3), and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. The statute's own mechanism is narrower than an outright disqualification of the whole exchange: property received outside these deadlines is treated as not like-kind, which triggers the boot-recognition and basis rules described elsewhere in this document rather than necessarily voiding nonrecognition treatment for property that was properly identified and received. No case law was researched for this clause; the deadlines are stated in unambiguous statutory text.

WHAT THIS NONRECOGNITION RULE DOES NOT COVER
Federal tax law places two real property exchanges outside § 1031's nonrecognition rule, on two different legal grounds. First, § 1031(a)(2) states that the nonrecognition rule does not apply to any exchange of real property held primarily for sale — property a dealer holds as inventory, rather than for productive use in a trade or business or for investment. Second, a separate provision, § 1031(h), states that real property located in the United States and real property located outside the United States are not property of a like kind to one another; an exchange of domestic for foreign real property therefore falls outside § 1031 because it fails the like-kind requirement itself, on different statutory grounds than the dealer-property exclusion in (a)(2), even though both are commonly described together as exclusions from the exchange rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This subsection shall not apply to any exchange of real property held primarily for sale."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, exclusion for dealer property held primarily for sale (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)
  "Real property located in the United States and real property located outside the United States are not property of a like kind."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1031(h) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, domestic and foreign real property not like kind (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as evidence of what § 1031 excludes generally — not tax advice about whether any specific property is dealer inventory or about where any specific replacement property is located. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, § 1031 — (a)(2) and (h) — and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. Correction to a common assumption: the foreign-real-property rule has never been housed within (a)(2)'s exclusion list; it has always been a separate provision (subsection (h), added in 1989) framed as a like-kind definition rather than an exclusion, and this structure predates the 2017 amendment. Before 2017, (a)(2) additionally excluded stocks, bonds, partnership interests, and several other categories of personal property from the exchange rule; those categories became moot for (a)(2) once the 2017 amendment limited § 1031 to real property generally, described in this document's clause on the core nonrecognition rule. No case law was researched for this clause.

BOOT AND BASIS CARRYOVER
If a taxpayer receives money or other non-like-kind property — commonly called "boot" — along with like-kind real property in a § 1031 exchange, 26 U.S.C. § 1031(b) states that any gain on the exchange is recognized, but only up to the amount of that money plus the fair market value of that other property; § 1031(c) states the parallel rule that a loss on the exchange is not recognized where boot is received. Separately, 26 U.S.C. § 1031(d) states that the taxpayer's basis in property acquired in the exchange is the same as the basis of the property given up, decreased by any money the taxpayer received and increased or decreased by any gain or loss recognized on the exchange; where the property received is partly like-kind replacement property and partly other property, that carried-over basis is allocated between them based on their relative fair market value at the date of the exchange.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "then the gain, if any, to the recipient shall be recognized, but in an amount not in excess of the sum of such money and the fair market value of such other property."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1031(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, gain recognized to the extent of boot received (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)
  "the basis shall be the same as that of the property exchanged, decreased in the amount of any money received by the taxpayer and increased in the amount of gain or decreased in the amount of loss to the taxpayer that was recognized on such exchange."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1031(d) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, basis of property received in the exchange (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1031)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as evidence of how § 1031 treats boot and basis generally — not tax advice computing the recognized gain or resulting basis for any specific taxpayer's exchange. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, § 1031 — (b) and (d) — and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. As the task instructions anticipated, this clause states the boot-recognition principle and the fact that basis carries over with adjustment at a factual level; it does not work through the basis-allocation formula in full technical detail. No case law was researched for this clause.

CALIFORNIA'S INFORMATION-RETURN REQUIREMENT FOR OUT-OF-STATE REPLACEMENT PROPERTY
California imposes its own tracking requirement on a taxpayer who defers California-source gain through a § 1031 exchange. Under California Revenue and Taxation Code § 18032 (personal income tax) and the parallel § 24953 (corporation tax), if gain or loss from an exchange of California real property is not recognized because of § 1031 of the Internal Revenue Code, and the replacement property acquired in that exchange is located outside California, the taxpayer must file an information return with the California Franchise Tax Board for the taxable year of the exchange and for each later taxable year in which that gain or loss remains unrecognized, in the form and manner the Franchise Tax Board prescribes. This is a reporting obligation, not a withholding tax collected out of the exchange proceeds: neither section requires money to be withheld under this particular provision. If a taxpayer fails to file this information return and also fails to file the income tax return otherwise required for that year, the Franchise Tax Board may estimate the taxpayer's net income from available information — including the deferred gain — and propose an assessment of tax, interest, and penalties. This filing requirement applies to exchanges occurring in taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2014.

  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 18032, California Revenue and Taxation Code, information return for California real property exchanged for out-of-state replacement property (personal income tax) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=18032.)
  "If gain or loss from the exchange of property in this state of a taxpayer is not recognized under this part because of Section 1031 of the Internal Revenue Code, relating to exchange of property held for productive use or investment, for a taxable year and the property acquired in that exchange is located outside of this state, the taxpayer shall file an information return with the Franchise Tax Board"
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 24953, California Revenue and Taxation Code, parallel information return requirement (corporation tax) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=24953.)

Correction to a common assumption: the mechanism the task described as "withholding" is, on the statutory text, an information-return filing requirement, not a withholding tax; California does have a separate, more general real-estate withholding statute (Rev. & Tax. Code § 18662) for certain California real property sales, but that provision is not part of this § 1031-specific tracking mechanism and was not researched for this document. Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 18032 and 24953 are separately codified sections — one under the Personal Income Tax Law, one under the Corporation Tax Law — rather than subsections of a single section, but they are near-identical mirror provisions enacted together by the same 2013 bill (Stats. 2013, Ch. 26 (AB 92)); they are cited together as confirmation that the same requirement reaches both individual and corporate taxpayers, not as fully independent corroboration of the underlying rule. The Franchise Tax Board's own form for this filing is commonly referred to as FTB Form 3840, "California Like-Kind Exchanges" — that form name and number come from the Franchise Tax Board's published guidance, not from the statutory text quoted below, and could not be independently verified against a primary ftb.ca.gov source in this research session because outbound access to ftb.ca.gov is blocked in this environment; it is stated here for reader orientation only, not as a verified citation. No case law was researched for this clause.

The Franchise Tax Board's own form for this filing is commonly referred to as FTB Form 3840, "California Like-Kind Exchanges" — that form name and number come from the Franchise Tax Board's published guidance, not from the statutory text quoted below, and could not be independently verified against a primary ftb.ca.gov source in this research session because outbound access to ftb.ca.gov is blocked in this environment; it is stated here for reader orientation only, not as a verified citation.
